title: The Cyrillic Stalemate: Why Uzbekistan’s Alphabet Reform is Still Stuck 30 Years Later
gist: More than 30 years after independence, Uzbekistan's official transition from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet remains incomplete, with the government having revised its alphabet policy multiple times while Cyrillic, Latin script, and the Russian language all continue to coexist in everyday public life.

insights.claim: Uzbekistan's transition from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet is not merely a technical change but is tied to the country's broader nation-building process since declaring independence in 1991.
insights.speaker: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
insights.so_what: Frames alphabet policy as a proxy for Uzbekistan's broader identity and geopolitical orientation (Turkic/Latin-script alignment vs. continued Russian-Cyrillic influence), relevant to long-term assessments of Tashkent's cultural and political alignment.
insights.quote: Uzbekistan’s transition from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet is not merely a technical change; rather, it has a far-reaching dimension tied to the nation-building process.

insights.claim: Since declaring independence in 1991, Tashkent has revised its alphabet policies numerous times, yet the simultaneous use of both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets has continued for over 30 years.
insights.speaker: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
insights.so_what: A three-decade policy stalemate signals weak state capacity or lack of political will to enforce a nominally completed reform, a useful indicator for assessing implementation risk of other Uzbek government initiatives.
insights.quote: Since declaring its independence in 1991, Tashkent has revised its alphabet policies numerous times, yet the simultaneous use of both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets has continued for over 30 years.

themes.theme: Everyday linguistic reality on the ground

insights.claim: Visitors to Uzbekistan still see both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets, alongside the Russian language written in Cyrillic, in many parts of daily life.
insights.speaker: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
insights.so_what: Persistent Russian-language and Cyrillic presence in daily commerce and administration indicates continued practical reliance on Russian-linked infrastructure and audiences, relevant to businesses and investors assessing linguistic/market access in Uzbekistan.
insights.quote: Visitors to Uzbekistan will still see both alphabets — alongside the Russian language, which uses a Cyrillic alphabet – in many parts of daily life.

insights.claim: The Latin script is now widely used for routine administrative, commercial and public signage, as illustrated by a roadside checkpoint sign reading 'Nazorat Posti 5' ('Checkpoint 5').
insights.speaker: Dolunay Yusuf Baltürk
insights.so_what: Latin script has taken over routine official signage even as Cyrillic and Russian persist elsewhere, indicating the transition is partial rather than absent — a two-track linguistic system rather than simple reform failure.
insights.quote: A roadside checkpoint marked “Nazorat Posti 5” (“Checkpoint 5”), photographed in Uzbekistan. The sign provides a simple example of the Latin script’s presence in everyday public life, where it is now widely used for routine administrative, commercial and public signage.
